name: Dusky Yellowish Green
lede: Dusky Yellowish Green is a dim, greyed olive green, built by stacking the modifiers dusky and yellowish onto the base color green rather than naming anything in particular.

sections.title: Two modifiers on green
sections.body:
Dusky Yellowish Green stacks two modifier words, dusky and yellowish, onto the base color [[green]], in the compound-modifier grammar ColorHub's library uses for names like this one rather than a borrowed object or place [1]. Ridgway's 1912 *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature* carries it as plate XLI, hue 29''', an aged plate scan read as approximate [1]. The ISCC-NBS dictionary of 1955 filed the same swatch under block 127, grayish olive green [1].

Its nearest named neighbor is [[dusky-green]], 2.6 units off, close enough to read as the same color on screen [1]; [[bronze-green]] sits 2.9 off and [[empire-green]] 4.4 [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds a color within six units of this swatch in 458 of 23,781 paintings, 1.93 percent, as photographed; looking inside each painting for at least five percent coverage narrows that to 259 [2]. That makes it more common than 75 percent of the named colors in our library [2]. It peaks in the 1900s, present in 4.1 percent of our 1,674 paintings from that decade, 3.5 times the museums' baseline rate [2]. Inside a painting it most often sits as a hidden color, in 46 percent of its 259 appearances by lightness rank [2].

Paul Gauguin is its most devoted painter on file, present in 7 of his 50 works here, several times the baseline rate for the museums that hold them [2]. The earliest match dates to 1301, six centuries before the name's 1912 record, so it marks a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not a surviving pigment [2]. It is most over-represented in paintings from France, and shares canvases with [[deep-slate-olive|Deep Olive-Grey]] more often than chance [2].
